query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of HfC and Ni to ZrB2 ceramic can lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.conditions: Hot pressing at 1750 °C for 1 h under 30 MPa in a vacuum
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a (Zr, Hf)B2 solid solution
generation.mechanism: Improved densification and refined microstructure due to the addition of HfC and Ni
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased flexural strength, hardness, and fracture toughness compared to conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 ceramic prepared at high temperatures (> 2300 °C)
generation.boundary: Preparation temperature, exposure time to liquid plating bath
generation.uncertainty: Optimal composition and processing conditions for the addition of HfC and Ni

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled preparation and testing of ZrB2-HfC-Ni ceramics with varying compositions and processing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of HfC and Ni does not result in improved mechanical properties and microstructure compared to conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, the hypothesis is falsified.

Over the years, numerous studies on the influence of Co–WC [], WSi2 [], ZrO2 fiber [], MoSi2 [], B4C [], and SiC [] additives on properties of ZrB2–based ceramic have been reported, whereas few studies on the effects of the HfC additive on properties of ZrB2–based ceramic have been undertaken.
ZrB2–based ceramics are commonly fabricated using the powder metallurgy technique. This technique mainly includes the solid phase sintering technique and liquid phase sintering technique. Compared to liquid phase sintering, solid phase sintering requires a higher sintering temperature. For solid phase sintering used in fabricating ZrB2–based ceramics, sintering temperature is usually about 2000 °C, such as 2200 °C for sintering ZrB2–TiB2 ceramics [], 2150–2250 °C for sintering ZrB2–B4C ceramics [], and 2000 °C for sintering ZrB2–SiC ceramics [], to obtain complete densification. ZrB2–10 wt % HfC–8 wt % Ni (ZH10N), ZrB2–20 wt % HfC–8 wt % Ni (ZH20N), and ZrB2–30 wt % HfC–8 wt % Ni (ZH30N) were hot pressed at 1750 °C for 1 h under 30 MPa in a vacuum (3 × 10−3 Pa).
Before hot pressing, powders were mixed and milled for 72 h in a polyethylene jar with zirconia balls and alcohol as medium. Then, the mixed slurry was dried in vacuum and sieved by a 200-mesh sieve. ## 3.1. Effects of HfC Addition on Microstructure of ZrB2–HfC Ceramics
Figure 1 shows the X-ray diffraction patterns of ZrB2–HfC ceramics. The main crystalline phases were ZrB2, HfC, and Ni, which was consistent with the compositions of the raw powders. This indicated that no reaction occurred during the sintering process. It can be seen that as HfC content increased, the peak of HfC increased accordingly.
Figure 2 exhibits SEM–BSE micrographs of polished surfaces of ZrB2–HfC ceramics with different HfC content. Obviously, ZrB2–HfC ceramics had three phases: A white phase, a black phase, and a grey phase. In order to determine their compositions, they were separately subjected to EDS analysis.
